title: Deck of Cards & Blackjack
summary: A reusable Card/Deck abstraction plus Blackjack's Ace-value ambiguity and a dealer state machine — two related but distinct interview prompts.

slides.markdown:
"Design a deck of cards" and "design Blackjack" sound like the same prompt, but they test different things — and interviewers ask both, sometimes as two stages of the same interview.

A deck of cards is a **reuse** problem: build `Card`, `Deck`, and `Hand` generically enough that Poker, War, and Blackjack can all sit on top without touching each other's rules. Blackjack on top of that is a **rules-and-state** problem: an Ace that's worth 1 or 11 depending on context, and a dealer that follows a fixed, non-negotiable procedure.

The skill being tested: keep the reusable primitives boring, and put all the game-specific cleverness in a layer above them.

**In scope:** a reusable `Card`/`Deck` abstraction (52-card deck, suits, ranks, shuffle, deal), plus Blackjack's rules on top — dealing two cards each, hitting, standing, busting past 21, and a dealer that plays a fixed strategy (hit until 17).

**Non-goals** unless asked: betting/wagering amounts, multiplayer tournaments with side pots, and card-counting detection (that's a common *follow-up*, not core scope — see interview questions).

State the two-layer scope out loud early: "I'll build generic card primitives first, then Blackjack rules on top of them" — it previews the exact structure the rest of the design follows and shows you're not planning to bake Blackjack logic into `Card` from line one.

Seven entities split across two layers. **Generic layer:** `Card` (suit + rank, immutable), `Deck` (52 cards, shuffle, deal), `Hand` (a player's held cards, generic add/list). **Blackjack layer:** `Shoe` (multiple decks combined, since casino Blackjack rarely deals from a single 52-card deck), `Player`, `Dealer` (a specialized player with a fixed strategy), `Game` (orchestrates a round).

The line to defend: `Hand` lives in the generic layer as a plain collection of cards, but **scoring** a hand is Blackjack-specific — so scoring is not a `Hand` method in the generic sense, it's added by the Blackjack layer (§ the hard part). Poker's hand-ranking would add its own scoring the same way, without touching `Card`, `Deck`, or `Hand`'s core shape.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: generic primitives vs Blackjack-specific rules
slides.markdown:
![Layered class diagram with Blackjack-specific classes depending downward on generic, reusable Card, Deck, and Hand classes](assets/layered-classes.svg)

The one-way dependency is the whole point: the bottom layer has zero imports from, or knowledge of, Blackjack. A second game (War, Poker) sits beside the Blackjack layer, both depending downward on the same `Card`/`Deck`/`Hand`, never on each other.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: the shared Deck and Hand contract
The hard part: scoring a hand with a flexible Ace
slides.markdown:
An Ace counts as **1 or 11**, whichever keeps the hand's total at or under 21 (or, if both bust, the smaller value). A naive implementation special-cases this per hand — "if there's exactly one Ace and the total would bust, subtract 10" — which breaks the moment a hand has two or three Aces.

The clean model: sum every card at its **hard** value (Ace = 11, face cards = 10), then count how many Aces are in the hand. While the total exceeds 21 and at least one Ace hasn't been "downgraded" yet, subtract 10 (treat one more Ace as 1 instead of 11) and repeat. This handles any number of Aces uniformly, with no per-hand special case.

A **soft** hand still has an Ace counted as 11; a **hard** hand has none (or all downgraded to 1).

![State machine for one Blackjack round moving through Betting, Dealing, PlayerTurns, DealerTurn, and Payout in a fixed sequence](assets/round-state-machine.svg)

The round only moves forward — there's no going back from `DealerTurn` to `PlayerTurns` once players have finished acting. That one-directional shape is what makes `Game` easy to reason about: at any moment there is exactly one current state, and the transition rules are fixed and small.

assets.alt: State machine for one Blackjack round moving through Betting, Dealing, PlayerTurns, DealerTurn, and Payout in a fixed sequence

slides.sectionTitle: Designing for reuse: War and Poker on the same primitives
slides.markdown:
War needs `Card`, `Deck`, and `Hand` exactly as built — it compares single card ranks, no scoring needed at all. Poker needs the same `Card`/`Deck`, plus its own hand-ranking logic (pairs, flushes, straights) layered the same way Blackjack layers `value()` on top of `Hand` — as a separate scorer or subtype, never as an edit to the generic `Hand` class.

The test for whether this reuse actually works: can you write a Poker `HandRanker` or a War `Game` without opening `Card.java`, `Deck.java`, or `Hand.java` at all? If yes, the layering held. If you find yourself adding a Poker-specific field to `Card`, the generic layer has already leaked game-specific concerns — see [strategy-pattern](strategy-pattern) for how a Strategy object formalizes this per-game variation.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: superclass with hooks vs a Strategy per game
slides.markdown:
| | `Game` superclass with hooks | Strategy object per game variant |
|---|---|---|
| Shape | `BlackjackGame extends Game`, overriding `dealInitialHand()`, `scoreHand()`, etc. | One `Game` class holding a `GameRules` strategy object; Blackjack and Poker each provide their own `GameRules` implementation |
| Adding a new game | New subclass, inherits the whole `Game` skeleton | New `GameRules` implementation, `Game` itself never changes |
| Risk | Deep inheritance chains get brittle as more games add more hook methods | Slightly more indirection to trace for a reader unfamiliar with the pattern |

**How to decide:** prefer the Strategy object once you have three or more game variants, or any variant that doesn't cleanly fit the hook sequence the first game assumed — composition scales better than inheritance here.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: putting Blackjack scoring inside Card
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Since Aces are worth 1 or 11 in Blackjack, I'll just give `Card` a `getBlackjackValue()` method."

**Why it's wrong:** a card's value is meaningless outside the context of a specific game and a specific hand — the same Ace is worth 1 point in one Blackjack scoring path and 14 in a high-Ace Poker variant. Putting `getBlackjackValue()` on `Card` bakes one game's rules into the layer every other card game is supposed to reuse, breaking the whole point of the split in §3.

**Correct model:** `Card` exposes only its intrinsic, game-agnostic identity (suit, rank). Scoring — Blackjack's soft/hard totals, Poker's hand ranks — lives entirely in that game's layer, reading a card's rank but never asking it for a game-specific value.
